specPoints.text: describe the evolution of stars of similar mass to the Sun through the following stages: • nebula • star (main sequence) • red giant • white dwarf

primer.text: Every Sun-sized star repeats the same biography: it condenses from a nebula into a protostar, ignites fusion as a main sequence star, swells into a red giant when the hydrogen runs low, and ends as a fading white dwarf. Learn the four stages in order and the physics at each turn.

lessons.title: From nebula to protostar
sourceHeadings: Summary of the life cycles of stars
lessons.opening: All stars begin inside a nebula — an enormous drifting cloud of gas and dust. Gravity draws the particles inward until a hot ball of gas forms — the protostar — whose density rises, collisions become more frequent, and temperature climbs.
keyPoints: Stars are born inside nebulae — enormous clouds of gas and dust drifting between the stars.
Gravity within the nebula pulls particles closer together.
The collapsing cloud becomes a hot ball of gas: a protostar.
As the protostar's density rises, more frequent collisions push its temperature up.

low.restatement: Nebula collapses under gravity → hot dense protostar → fusion ignites.
low.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill gathers itself tighter and warms from the squeezing — then finally 'lights up'.
low.examPointer: Sequence questions want the arrow order; the nebula always comes first.

medium.restatement: Collapse concentrates particles, so collision frequency — and therefore temperature — climbs until fusion can start.
medium.analogy: Pumping a bicycle pump: compressing the air inside warms it.
medium.examPointer: Tie density up → collisions up → temperature up in one sentence for the explanation mark.

check.stem: Stars begin their lives as…

options.text: a nebula — a giant cloud of gas and dust
options.explanation: The nebula is stage one for every star.
White dwarfs are the end of the road, not the start.
Red giants come after the main sequence.
Supernovae end the largest stars' lives.

check.stem: What force pulls a nebula into a protostar?

options.text: gravity, pulling the particles closer together
options.explanation: Gravity drives the collapse.
Gravity, not magnetism, does the gathering.
Light pressure is not the collapsing agent.
Fusion starts only after the protostar is hot enough.

check.stem: As the protostar's density increases, its temperature…

options.text: increases, because collisions between particles become more frequent
options.explanation: More crowding means more collisions and more heating.

options.text: decreases, because the particles spread out
options.explanation: Collapsing crowds particles, it does not spread them.
The temperature climbs during collapse.
Nothing cools to zero here.

check.stem: A protostar becomes a main sequence star when…

options.text: it becomes hot enough for nuclear fusion to begin in its core
options.explanation: Fusion ignition is the promotion criterion.
Running out comes billions of years later.

options.text: it collapses into a white dwarf
options.explanation: That is the solar-mass ending.
Only the most massive stars do that.

check.stem: Which sequence opens a star's life story, starting from a nebula?

options.explanation: All stars follow the same opening stages.
The nebula comes first.
The red giant is a late stage.
The main sequence follows ignition.

check.stem: State what a nebula is.
check.modelAnswer: A nebula is an enormous drifting cloud of gas and dust, and stars form inside it.

check.stem: Describe how a protostar forms.
check.modelAnswer: Gravity draws the nebula's particles inward until a hot ball of gas forms — the protostar.

check.stem: Explain why a collapsing protostar gets hotter.
check.modelAnswer: As gravity packs the particles closer, the density rises and collisions between particles become more frequent, and those more frequent collisions raise the temperature.

check.stem: A cloud of gas is collapsing. State the stage it has reached once it is a hot, dense ball but fusion has not yet started.
check.modelAnswer: It is a protostar: fusion ignition, which would promote it to a main sequence star, has not yet begun.

lessons.title: Main sequence and red giant
lessons.opening: Once fusion ignites, the star joins the main sequence and holds itself in stable equilibrium. After several billion years the hydrogen begins to run out, core fusion dies down, and the star fuses helium instead — swelling outward and cooling into a red giant.
keyPoints: A star that initiates fusion is a main sequence star, in stable equilibrium.
Several billion years in, the hydrogen begins to run low.
The core fusion reactions die down, and the star begins fusing helium.
Helium fusion makes the outer star expand; the cooling surface turns it into a red giant.

low.restatement: Fusion ignites → stable main sequence → hydrogen fades → helium fusion swells the star into a red giant.
low.analogy: A log fire: steady burn (main sequence), then the logs collapse and the flames spread wide but cooler (red giant).
low.examPointer: Six-mark lifecycle answers score on order — always name the fuel that changes at each turn.

medium.restatement: The red giant turn is a fuel story: hydrogen exhaustion switches the core to helium, and the swelling surface cools and reddens.
medium.analogy: A balloon inflating as the air inside is rearranged — bigger outside, cooler at the skin.
medium.examPointer: 'Red giant' then 'white dwarf' — never insert a supernova for a Sun-mass star.

check.stem: A main sequence star is stable because…

options.text: it is in equilibrium during its fusion-powered life
options.explanation: Equilibrium is the main-sequence state.
Fusion is what powers the main sequence.
Expansion belongs to the red giant stage.
Collapse ended at the protostar stage.

check.stem: What triggers the red giant stage?

options.text: the hydrogen in the core beginning to run out
options.explanation: Fuel exhaustion starts the transition.

options.text: the star colliding with a nebula
options.explanation: Collisions are not part of the sequence.
Solar-mass stars never explode.
Helium fusion is what happens next, not what stops.

check.stem: During the red giant stage the star…

options.text: expands outward as its surface cools
options.explanation: Helium fusion swells the outer layers; expansion cools them.
That describes the white dwarf turn.
The star swells dramatically.
Hydrogen is fading, not accelerating.

check.stem: After the main sequence, a Sun-like star becomes…

options.explanation: Red giant precedes the white dwarf for solar-mass stars.
Only much larger stars go supernova.
That follows supernovae of big stars.
Stages do not rewind.

check.stem: The star begins to fuse which fuel as it turns into a red giant?

options.explanation: Helium fusion swells the outer layers.
Carbon comes later, in larger stars.
Iron belongs to the most massive stars.
Uranium is a fission fuel, not a stellar fuel.

check.stem: State the stage a star enters once fusion starts in its core.
check.modelAnswer: It becomes a main sequence star and is in stable equilibrium.

check.stem: Name the stage after the main sequence for a Sun-like star.
check.modelAnswer: The star becomes a red giant.

check.stem: Explain why the star expands when the red giant stage begins.
check.modelAnswer: With the hydrogen fading, the star starts fusing helium, and those reactions push the outer layers outward — the star swells while its surface cools.

check.stem: A star has burned most of its core hydrogen. State the next two stages it passes through.
check.modelAnswer: It next becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf.

lessons.title: The white dwarf ending
lessons.opening: When the helium fusion reactions finish, the star collapses into a white dwarf. The white dwarf cools over time, so the energy it emits decreases, until the faded remnant gives out no light at all — the black dwarf stage.
keyPoints: Once helium fusion finishes, the star collapses into a white dwarf.
White dwarfs cool steadily as the ages pass.
As it cools, the energy a white dwarf emits decreases.
A fully faded white dwarf that no longer emits light is a black dwarf.

low.restatement: Fusion ends → collapse → white dwarf, which cools and fades toward black.
low.analogy: A charcoal briquette after the fire: still glowing (white dwarf), then greyer and darker as the night wears on (black dwarf).
low.examPointer: White dwarf cools and dims — keep 'black dwarf' only for the no-light endpoint.

medium.restatement: The endpoint is radiative retirement: no fuel, no fusion, just cooling and dimming.
medium.analogy: An unplanned power cut in a city: the lights fade as the stored energy drains.
medium.examPointer: Emission decreases as temperature decreases — write both clauses.

check.stem: What does a solar-mass star become when helium fusion ends?

options.text: a white dwarf, as the star collapses
options.explanation: Collapse after helium exhaustion forms the white dwarf.
Stages do not repeat backwards.
Solar-mass stars shed no supernova.
Black holes need far more mass.

check.stem: Over time a white dwarf…

options.text: cools down and emits decreasing energy
options.explanation: Cooling is the white dwarf's whole career.
It cools, it does not climb.
The fuel is gone.
No re-expansion happens.

check.stem: A black dwarf is…

options.text: a white dwarf that has cooled until it no longer emits light
options.explanation: The fully faded endpoint carries the 'black' name.
It is the cooled endpoint of a formed star.

options.text: a nebula ready to form stars
options.explanation: Nebulae are birthplaces, not endings.

options.text: another name for a black hole
options.explanation: Black holes form from the most massive stars.

check.stem: What does a solar-mass star collapse into once helium fusion finishes?

options.text: a white dwarf, once helium fusion finishes
options.explanation: Collapse follows the end of helium fusion.

options.text: main sequence → white dwarf → red giant
options.explanation: The dwarf comes last.

options.text: red giant → main sequence → white dwarf
options.explanation: The main sequence comes first.
That is the large-star path.

check.stem: As the white dwarf cools, the energy it emits…

options.explanation: Cooling output falls in step with temperature.
Cooling means less emission.
The emission declines as it cools.
Nothing restarts high-energy emission.

check.stem: State what a star becomes when its helium fusion finishes.
check.modelAnswer: Collapse sets in, and the star becomes a white dwarf.

check.stem: State what a white dwarf eventually becomes.
check.modelAnswer: It cools until it no longer emits light and becomes a black dwarf.

check.stem: Explain why a white dwarf's light output falls over time.
check.modelAnswer: The white dwarf has no fusion left to feed it, so it simply cools; as its temperature drops, the energy it emits decreases until it no longer emits light.

check.stem: Order the full solar-mass biography: white dwarf, nebula, red giant, main sequence star.
check.modelAnswer: Nebula → main sequence star → red giant → white dwarf.

glossary.definition: An enormous cloud of gas and dust drifting between the stars, where stars are born.
The hot, dense ball of gas formed as gravity collapses a nebula.
A star in stable equilibrium once fusion has begun in its core.
The collapsed, cooling endpoint of a solar-mass star.

figures.alt: Flowchart showing star life cycle: gas cloud becomes protostar, then main sequence star. The paths then split, demonstrating that a star about the same size as the Sun will become a red giant,  white dwarf, and black dwarf. A star much bigger than the Sun will become a red supergiant, supernova, and either a neutron star or a black hole.
